title: The Network Edge: Hosts, Access Networks, Physical Media

questions.q: Why are the end devices at the network's edge (laptops, phones, servers, cars, smart appliances) called hosts?
choices: They host the routing tables used to forward other users' packets
They host (run) network applications
They are hosted inside the ISP's network core
They host the base stations of the access network
questions.explain: End systems are called hosts because they host, or run, network applications. A host can be a client, which requests and receives a service, or a server, which provides one.

questions.q: Which statements correctly describe hosts at the network edge?
choices: A client host requests and receives a service
Hosts are the interconnected routers that form a network of networks
A server host provides a service
Servers are often located in data centers
questions.explain: Hosts are clients and servers, and servers often sit in data centers. Interconnected routers forming a network of networks make up the network core, not the edge.

questions.q: Which description fits the network core?
choices: The hosts that run network applications
The links between a home and its cable headend or central office
Interconnected routers forming a network of networks
The wireless base stations that phones attach to
questions.explain: The core is the mesh of interconnected routers. Separately run networks (ISPs, content provider networks, and so on) are interconnected there, which makes the Internet a network of networks. Hosts, access links and base stations belong to the edge and access networks.

questions.q: What does an access network do?
choices: Connects an end system, or a whole network such as a home network, to its first-hop (edge) router
Interconnects the routers of national and global ISPs
Runs network applications for clients
Stores content in data centers close to users
questions.explain: The access network is the network that connects an end system to the first-hop router on the path from source to destination. In some cases it connects a whole network, such as a home network, to the larger Internet.

questions.q: Which are the broad categories of access networks?
choices: Residential access networks (e.g., cable, DSL)
Institutional access networks (e.g., school, company)
Router-to-router core networks
Mobile access networks (e.g., WiFi, 4G/5G)
questions.explain: There are three types of access networks: residential, institutional (run by a company, school or municipality) and mobile (cellular carriers and WiFi). Router-to-router networks make up the core.

questions.q: When you compare access network technologies, which two questions matter most?
choices: Which vendor built it, and how old is it?
How many core routers does it pass through, and how far apart are they?
Which applications does it allow, and which does it block?
What is its transmission rate, and is the access shared with other users or dedicated?
questions.explain: The two things to compare are the bit transmission rate (how fast the network is) and how much one user has to share the network with other users. For example, cable is shared and DSL is dedicated.

questions.q: A cable network carries TV channels and data channels over the same cable by sending them in different frequency bands. What is this technique called?
questions.explain: Frequency division multiplexing (FDM) sends different channels in different frequency bands. They don't interfere with each other, much as FM radio stations broadcast on different frequencies.

questions.q: Cable-based access is called HFC. What does HFC stand for?
questions.explain: HFC stands for hybrid fiber coax. A network of coaxial cable and fiber connects homes to the ISP router.

questions.q: Which equipment at the cable headend terminates the connections from the homes' cable modems?
choices: DSLAM (DSL access multiplexer)
CMTS (cable modem termination system)
WiFi access point
Ethernet switch
questions.explain: The cable modem termination system (CMTS) at the headend connects the shared cable distribution network to the ISP. The DSLAM does the same job for DSL, but it is located in a telephone central office.

questions.q: Your cable internet slows down every evening when your neighbors are streaming a lot. Which property of cable access best explains this?
choices: Each home's line to the central office loses capacity with distance
Cable is symmetric, so neighbors' uploads use up your download capacity
Homes share the cable distribution network to the headend, and may share a frequency channel
Coax can carry only one channel at a time
questions.explain: Cable access is a shared network: homes share the access network to the cable headend, and neighbors may share a frequency. Heavy use by a neighbor can cut into what you can send and receive. Losing capacity with distance is a DSL issue, and coax carries many frequency channels.

questions.q: Which transmission rates are typical of cable (HFC) access?
choices: 24 to 52 Mbps downstream; 3.5 to 16 Mbps upstream
About 10 Gbps in both directions
40 Mbps to 1.2 Gbps downstream; 30 to 100 Mbps upstream
11, 54 or 450 Mbps in both directions
questions.explain: HFC is asymmetric: up to 40 Mbps to 1.2 Gbps downstream and 30 to 100 Mbps upstream. The 24-52 / 3.5-16 Mbps figures are for DSL, and 11/54/450 Mbps are WiFi rates.

questions.q: In cable access, each home has its own dedicated cable that runs all the way to the cable headend.
questions.explain: One physical cable connects many homes to a single headend. Data and TV travel at different frequencies over a shared cable distribution network. A dedicated line to the provider is what DSL offers.

questions.q: Which physical line does DSL use to reach the home?
choices: A shared coaxial cable that runs past many homes to a cable headend
The existing telephone line (twisted-pair copper) to the telephone company's central office
A dedicated fiber to the ISP's core routers
A point-to-point terrestrial microwave link
questions.explain: DSL uses the existing phone line, a twisted pair of copper wires, which runs directly to the central office's DSLAM.

questions.q: In DSL access, what device in the central office do the subscribers' phone lines connect to? (Give its abbreviation.)
questions.explain: The DSLAM (DSL access multiplexer) in the central office sends DSL data toward the ISP and the Internet, and sends voice toward the telephone network.

questions.q: Voice and data share a DSL phone line on the way to the central office. Where does each go from there?
choices: Data goes on to the Internet (via the ISP)
Voice and data both go to the cable headend
Voice goes on to the telephone network
Data goes to the telephone network and voice goes to the Internet
questions.explain: Data sent over the DSL phone line goes to the Internet, and voice goes to the telephone network. Cable headends belong to cable access, not DSL.

questions.q: How can one DSL phone line carry voice calls and Internet data at the same time?
choices: Voice is sent only when no data is waiting
Data travels over a fiber inside the phone line while voice uses the copper
Voice and data are transmitted at different frequencies
The DSLAM compresses voice into the data stream before it reaches the home
questions.explain: Voice and data travel at different frequencies over the dedicated line to the central office, so they don't interfere.

questions.q: DSL transmission rates depend strongly on the distance between the home and the central office. Beyond roughly 3 miles, DSL generally isn't possible.
questions.explain: DSL rates fall off with distance from the central office. If the home is too far away (generally more than about three miles), DSL to the central office isn't possible.

questions.q: Compared with cable, how would you describe DSL's transmission capacity between the home and the central office?
choices: Shared with every home on the same street
Dedicated: not shared with neighbors
Symmetric: the same rate in both directions
Hundreds of Gbps in each direction
questions.explain: Each DSL line runs directly to the central office, so you don't share capacity with neighbors on that stretch. DSL is still asymmetric: 24-52 Mbps dedicated downstream and 3.5-16 Mbps dedicated upstream.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: In a typical home network, which of these functions are often combined in a single box?
choices: Cable or DSL modem
DSLAM
Router (with firewall and NAT)
CMTS
WiFi wireless access point
questions.explain: A home network has a cable or DSL modem leading to the headend or central office, a router (firewall, NAT), and a WiFi access point plus wired Ethernet. These are often combined in one box. The DSLAM and CMTS are on the provider's side.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: The word "modem" is short for which two words?
questions.explain: Modem is short for modulator-demodulator. It sits at the house end of the cable or DSL link.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: What usually distinguishes an enterprise network (company, university) from a home network?
choices: It uses only wireless links
It connects to the Internet without a router
It has no servers of its own
It has multiple switches and routers to handle a large number of devices
questions.explain: An enterprise network is like a home network on steroids: a mix of wired Ethernet and WiFi, with multiple switches and routers for the many connected devices. It often has its own institutional mail and web servers too.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: Which rates are typical for wired Ethernet access in an enterprise network?
choices: 11, 54 and 450 Mbps
100 Mbps, 1 Gbps and 10 Gbps
24 to 52 Mbps
1 to 2 Mbps
questions.explain: Enterprise Ethernet provides wired access at 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps and 10 Gbps. The 11/54/450 Mbps figures are WiFi access point rates.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: What characterizes data center networks?
choices: High-bandwidth links (10s to 100s of Gbps) connecting hundreds to thousands of servers to each other and to the Internet
A shared coaxial cable connecting servers to a cable headend
Low-rate Bluetooth links between nearby servers
A dedicated telephone line from each server to a central office
questions.explain: Data center networks connect very large numbers of servers to each other and to the Internet over high-bandwidth links of 10s to 100s of Gbps.

questions.category: Home, enterprise, and data center networks
questions.q: An enterprise network typically mixes wired (Ethernet) and wireless (WiFi) link technologies.
questions.explain: Enterprise networks use a mix of wired and wireless links (Ethernet at 100 Mbps-10 Gbps, WiFi at 11/54/450 Mbps), connecting a mix of switches and routers.

questions.q: In a shared wireless access network, end systems connect to the router through a base station, also called a(n) ________.
questions.explain: Both WLANs and cellular networks connect end devices through a base station, also called an access point. The end devices send data to it and receive data from it.

questions.q: WiFi wireless LANs are standardized under which IEEE family of protocols? (Give the number.)
questions.explain: WiFi is the IEEE 802.11 family. 802.11b/g/n correspond to rates of 11, 54 and 450 Mbps.

questions.q: WiFi (wireless LAN) protocols are standardized by the IETF.
questions.explain: WiFi protocols are standardized by the IEEE as the 802.11 family, not by the IETF.

questions.q: Which of these describe wide-area cellular access networks (e.g., 4G/5G) rather than wireless LANs?
choices: Usually confined to within or around a building
Provided by a mobile cellular network operator
Standardized as IEEE 802.11b/g/n
Coverage measured in tens of kilometers
questions.explain: Cellular access is provided by mobile cellular operators and covers 10s of km. WLANs (WiFi, IEEE 802.11) usually cover the inside of a building and the area around it.

questions.q: A student's phone streams music while she rides a bus across town, and it stays connected for the whole trip. Which access network is she most likely using?
choices: Wireless LAN (WiFi)
DSL
Wide-area cellular (4G/5G)
Bluetooth
questions.explain: Only wide-area cellular access covers tens of kilometers. A WiFi LAN covers about a building, Bluetooth reaches only a few meters, and DSL is a wired residential link.

questions.q: How does a host send an application message into the access network?
choices: It sends the whole message as one continuous stream with no added information
It breaks the message into smaller chunks (packets) of L bits, each with a header, and transmits them at the link's transmission rate R
It waits for the first-hop router to request each byte
It turns the whole message into a single radio pulse
questions.explain: The host's sending function takes the application message and breaks it into packets of length L bits. Each packet carries a header whose contents are set by a protocol. The host transmits each packet into the access network at transmission rate R.

questions.q: The link transmission rate R is also called:
choices: Link capacity
Propagation delay
Link bandwidth
Packet length
questions.explain: R, in bits per second, is the link transmission rate, also called link capacity or link bandwidth. Packet length is L, and propagation delay is a different quantity.

questions.q: A host sends a 1,500-byte packet into a 100 Mbps link. What is the packet transmission delay, in microseconds? (Use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bits/s.)
How many milliseconds does it take to transmit a 1,500-byte packet into a 2 Mbps link, such as a slow cellular connection? (Use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bits/s.)
questions.explain: L = 12,000 bits. L/R = 12,000 / (2 x 10^6) s = 0.006 s = 6 ms. The same packet on 1 Gbps Ethernet would take only 12 microseconds.

questions.q: A host sends two 1,500-byte packets back to back into a 10 Mbps link. How many milliseconds does it take to transmit both? (Use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bits/s.)
questions.explain: Each packet is 12,000 bits, so both together are 24,000 bits. 24,000 / (10 x 10^6) s = 0.0024 s = 2.4 ms (1.2 ms per packet).

questions.q: Transmitting a 1,000-byte packet into a link takes 80 microseconds. What is the link's transmission rate, in Mbps? (Use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bits/s.)
questions.explain: Rearrange delay = L/R to R = L/delay = 8,000 bits / (80 x 10^-6 s) = 10^8 bits/s = 100 Mbps.

questions.q: If both the packet length L and the link transmission rate R double, what happens to the packet transmission delay?
choices: It doubles
It halves
It quadruples
It stays the same
questions.explain: Transmission delay = L/R, and (2L)/(2R) = L/R. Doubling only R would halve the delay, and doubling only L would double it.

questions.q: A packet contains only a chunk of application data; protocols add no extra information to it.
questions.explain: Besides the data, each packet carries a header, and a protocol dictates exactly what goes into it. The packet (data plus header) is L bits long.

questions.q: Which of these are guided media?
choices: Twisted-pair copper
WiFi radio
Coaxial cable
Satellite radio link
Fiber optic cable
questions.explain: In guided media, signals propagate through a solid medium: copper (twisted pair), coax or fiber. Radio links such as WiFi and satellite are unguided, because their signals propagate freely.

questions.q: What is the difference between guided and unguided media?
choices: Guided media have a router at each end; unguided media do not
Guided media carry only analog signals; unguided media carry only digital signals
In guided media, signals propagate through a solid medium (copper, fiber, coax); in unguided media, signals propagate freely (e.g., radio)
Guided media are always shared; unguided media are always dedicated
questions.explain: Guided means the signal is confined to a physical wire or cable. Unguided means the signal propagates freely, like radio. In both cases the physical link is whatever lies between the transmitter and the receiver.

questions.q: Which Ethernet rates do Category 5 and Category 6 twisted pair support?
choices: Cat 5: 10 Gbps; Cat 6: 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps
Cat 5: 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps; Cat 6: 10 Gbps
Both: 11, 54 and 450 Mbps
Cat 5: 45 Mbps; Cat 6: 1.2 Gbps
questions.explain: Twisted pair is two insulated copper wires. Category 5 supports 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps Ethernet, and Category 6 supports 10 Gbps Ethernet.

questions.q: Coaxial cable is described as "broadband." What does that mean here?
choices: It broadcasts signals freely through the air
It is a wide glass fiber
It can carry only one high-rate channel
It carries multiple frequency channels on the cable, at 100s of Mbps per channel
questions.explain: Coax (two concentric copper conductors, bidirectional) is broadband: it carries multiple frequency channels, each at 100s of Mbps. This is what lets cable access use FDM.

questions.q: Which medium is made of two concentric copper conductors and is bidirectional?
choices: Twisted pair
Coaxial cable
Fiber optic cable
Terrestrial microwave
questions.explain: Coaxial cable has two concentric copper conductors. Twisted pair is two insulated copper wires twisted around each other, and fiber is glass that carries light pulses.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons fiber optic cable has a low error rate?
choices: It is immune to electromagnetic noise
Its transmitters and receivers are cheaper than copper equipment
Repeaters can be spaced far apart
It broadcasts to every nearby receiver
questions.explain: Fiber's low error rate comes with repeaters spaced far apart and immunity to electromagnetic noise. Fiber also runs at 10s-100s of Gbps point to point. Its drawback is that its transmitting and receiving components tend to cost more than copper's.

questions.q: Fiber optic cable is glass fiber that carries light. Each light ________ represents one bit.
questions.explain: Fiber carries light pulses, and each pulse is a bit.

questions.q: Which of these make wireless radio a harsh environment for transmitting bits?
choices: Reflection off objects
Obstruction (blocking) by objects
Interference and noise, e.g., from motors and microwave ovens
Signal fading over distance
Immunity to electromagnetic noise
questions.explain: Radio signals fade over distance, reflect off objects, can be blocked by objects (or pass through walls, depending on frequency), and pick up noise from motors, microwaves and other RF sources. Immunity to electromagnetic noise is a property of fiber.

questions.q: Wireless radio transmissions are broadcast. Which concerns does this raise?
choices: Signals can reach only a single pre-wired receiver
Bits must first be converted to light pulses
Eavesdropping and interference, since nearby devices may receive or disrupt the signal
Each device needs its own dedicated wire
questions.explain: Wireless has no physical wire. Bits are modulated onto a signal in a frequency band of the electromagnetic spectrum and broadcast, so any nearby device may receive them. That raises eavesdropping and interference concerns.

questions.q: Which radio link type is meant as a cable replacement, with short distances and limited rates?
choices: Terrestrial microwave
4G/5G cellular
Satellite
Bluetooth
questions.explain: Bluetooth replaces cables. It runs at low rates (about 1-2 Mbps max) over short ranges, usually no more than 5-10 meters.

questions.q: Which description fits terrestrial microwave links?
choices: Point-to-point links with 45 Mbps channels
Broadcast to every device in a building at 450 Mbps
A cable-replacement technology with a range of a few meters
Links through a geostationary satellite with about 270 ms of delay
questions.explain: Terrestrial microwave is point-to-point, with 45 Mbps channels. The other options describe WiFi, Bluetooth and geostationary satellite links.

questions.q: About how much end-to-end delay does a link through a geostationary satellite have?
choices: 27 microseconds
2.7 ms
270 ms
questions.explain: Geostationary satellite links have a noticeable delay of about 270 ms, caused by the long distance the signal must travel.

questions.q: The roughly 270 ms delay of a geostationary satellite link is the time it takes to push a packet's bits onto the link, so sending smaller packets would remove most of it.
questions.explain: The 270 ms is propagation delay: the time from when a bit is sent at the sender to when it is received at the receiver, over a very long distance. Transmission delay (L/R) is the time to push a packet's bits into the link. Smaller packets reduce transmission delay but not propagation delay.

questions.q: Which ordering of radio link types goes from shortest to longest typical range?
choices: WiFi < Bluetooth < 4G/5G cellular
Bluetooth < WiFi < 4G/5G cellular
4G/5G cellular < WiFi < Bluetooth
Bluetooth < 4G/5G cellular < WiFi
questions.explain: Bluetooth reaches a few meters (about 5-10 m), WiFi reaches 10s of meters, and cellular covers about 10 km or more.
